- What gets automated depends on how controlled the setting is, not on how hard the task looks (The same physical task falls on either side of the line depending on its surroundings. A car plant fits windscreens with robots, while replacing the same glass in a garage uses a technician, because removing a broken screen and preparing the frame demands adaptation no affordable robot manages. Amazon's Kiva robots automated the warehouse by moving shelves across a level floor while a person still does the picking. Minsky states it from the other side, since mathematical logic fell to a program in 1956 and college calculus in 1961 while what a four-year-old does resisted for decades. Both claims count as evidence, but the price of making a setting controlled is usually invisible and enormous.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-what-gets-automated-depends-on-how-controlled-the-setting-is-not-on-how-hard-the
- A person can direct work they could not do themselves by comparing results instead of producing them (Judging between two finished attempts is easier than making one, so a person can push work toward what they want without being able to do it. The single claim behind this comes from Christian's The Alignment Problem: Christiano, Leike and Amodei's simulated leg learned a tucked backflip from a few hundred either-or choices, about an hour of one person's time, and nobody involved could have performed the move. One simulated robot carries the whole thesis, so it stands on thin evidence. The method also assumes the chooser knows what they want, and where all the choices were collected before training the agent kept the loopholes it found.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-a-person-can-direct-work-they-could-not-do-themselves-by-comparing-results-inste
- What defeats adding people to a project is the cost of coordinating them, not their individual ability (Each person added has to be trained by those already working, and the talking grows faster than the headcount, so the work does not divide. Brooks states it flatly: adding people to a late software project makes it later. Weinberg's rule of thumb, that three programmers do about twice the work of one, points the same way, and his correction of the famous thirty-to-one gap between programmers, which came from comparing the best person on one task with the worst on another, supplies the other half. No claim here counts as evidence, three are opinion and two contested, and Weinberg's numbers are asserted rather than measured.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-what-defeats-adding-people-to-a-project-is-the-cost-of-coordinating-them-not-the
- Some failures come from how the machine reads the input, so no rewording fixes them (Asked how many Ds are in DEEPSEEK, DeepSeek-V3 answered 2 or 3 across ten tries, because the word arrives as the chunks D, EEP, SEE and K rather than as letters. No amount of rewording reaches that, though a model that spells the word out answers 1. Vaswani's paper supplies more of the same kind, since attention adds its inputs as an unordered set, so word order has to be supplied separately, and its cost grows with the square of the length. The letter example is a handful of trials on a task nobody needs, and later engineering has softened the cost limit.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-some-failures-come-from-how-the-machine-reads-the-input-so-no-rewording-fixes-th
- A model only helps where it gets right the cases the person gets wrong, and hurts elsewhere (Bansal found that a model scoring about as well as a person is not thereby a useful partner. The pair beats either one alone only where the model is right on the particular cases the person gets wrong. Dell'Acqua measured the other side. On a case built to fall just outside what the model handles well, 373 consultants were right 84.4 per cent of the time alone, 70.6 per cent with the model and 60.0 per cent with prompt training as well. Both results are constructed, since Bansal matched the accuracies by design, and Vaccaro's 2024 pooling of 106 experiments suggests that match is a narrow condition rather than a usual one.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-a-model-only-helps-where-it-gets-right-the-cases-the-person-gets-wrong-and-hurts
- A famous result gets quoted far more widely than the study behind it can support (The studies behind well-known results are often small or run in one setting, and the headline drops those limits. Anthropic's tracing method gave a usable picture on about a quarter of the prompts tried, and it reads a stand-in model rather than the real one; Hoffmann's scaling prediction rests on small models and one full-scale run. Bucinca tested one low-stakes nutrition task with online workers and then assumed the result holds for experts. Asch's conformity rate moves with the decade and the country, and most of his own subjects held out. None of this makes the findings wrong, only the quoting wider than the measuring.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-a-famous-result-gets-quoted-far-more-widely-than-the-study-behind-it-can-support
- A person builds the problem out of a confusing situation and no technique performs that step (Schön argues that problems do not arrive ready-made. Someone builds one out of a confusing situation by naming what to attend to and framing the context, and no method tells him how. Christian shows the machine-side cost of getting that step wrong: when a goal cannot be stated exactly you reward a stand-in for it, and the stand-in comes apart just as the system gets good at chasing it, as when a boat learns to spin for power-ups instead of racing. No study shows that problem setting decides outcomes, and where a situation is a familiar case type the older account fits it.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-a-person-builds-the-problem-out-of-a-confusing-situation-and-no-technique-perfor
- A person needs enough skill to produce the machine's answer before they can check it (Asked why they had not thought about an output, 319 workers gave 152 reasons of awareness and 130 of ability, against only 44 who said they had no time, while 83 said they trusted the tool and 58 lacked the knowledge to inspect it. Vaccaro's team argue that the real job in these setups is deciding whose answer to use, and someone who cannot tell a hard case from an easy one cannot tell when the machine is wrong. Lee and See draw the design conclusion that a weaker tool you can check may be worth more than a stronger one you cannot. Two of the three claims are argument rather than measurement.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-a-person-needs-enough-skill-to-produce-the-machine-s-answer-before-they-can-chec
- How a model is trained matters more than how big it is (Ouyang's raters preferred InstructGPT at 1.3 billion parameters to the 175-billion-parameter GPT-3 it was built from, so a small amount of human ranking bought more obedience than a hundredfold increase in size. Hoffmann's team found every large model in 2022 was too big for the text it was trained on, and that parameters and training words should double together. Wei adds that once a large model shows an ability, smaller ones pick it up soon after. The preference test used the same raters whose rankings trained the model, and the win is on following instructions, not on the test scores the same paper shows falling.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-how-a-model-is-trained-matters-more-than-how-big-it-is
- Damasio says a gut feeling cuts the options down before reasoning starts, and people who lose it decide badly (A feeling attached to an imagined outcome arrives before the options are weighed, and it drops most of them. Damasio's patient Elliot scored superior or average on every intelligence test and still spent half an hour listing reasons for and against two appointment dates without choosing. Eleven further patients with the same prefrontal damage showed the same pairing of lost feeling and lost judgement, and healthy card players sweat before a risky deck while these patients do not. The general point was accepted but the particular mechanism was not; several of the card-game results have been reassigned since, and that dispute is the claim standing against.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-damasio-says-a-gut-feeling-cuts-the-options-down-before-reasoning-starts-and-peo
- Grief comes from what you were told and from calling something mine, not from what happened in the world (The Pañcadaśī's pair does the work: a father whose son is alive abroad weeps at a liar's word that the boy is dead, while a father whose son has really died does not weep because the news has not reached him. The two differ only in what they were told. The Yoga Vasistha adds the second half, three fighters made without conditioning who could not be killed until the gods put the feelings of I and mine into them. Nothing is measured, both are constructed stories, and Vidyāraṇya blocks the idealist reading himself by saying the world in the mind still needs the outer one as its basis.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-grief-comes-from-what-you-were-told-and-from-calling-something-mine-not-from-wha
- How well workers feel they did points the opposite way from the measurement, and experience does not fix it (METR's trial is the sharpest case. The same developers predicted AI would make them 24 per cent faster and said afterwards it had made them 20 per cent faster, but measured they were 19 per cent slower, and months of using the tool did not shrink the error. Outside experts were wrong in the same direction and further, with economists predicting 39 per cent faster and machine learning researchers 38. Shen and Tamkin's assisted workers found the task easier and rated the quiz afterwards exactly as hard as everyone else did, and Reeves and Nass found self-report the reverse of behaviour every time. The METR offset rests on sixteen developers doing one kind of work.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-how-well-workers-feel-they-did-points-the-opposite-way-from-the-measurement-and-
- Computers cut middle-paying jobs and move work to both ends of the scale while pay does not follow (The jobs computers take sit in the middle of the pay scale, so employment grows at the top and the bottom, and the pay at the bottom does not rise with it. Autor's figures carry it: the four middle-skill American occupation groups fell from sixty per cent of employment in 1979 to forty-nine in 2007, and across sixteen European economies between 1993 and 2010 the middle-paying share fell in every single country. Real wages below roughly the fifteenth percentile fell between 1999 and 2007 even as those jobs grew. Both claims come from one author, so it stands on thin evidence, and a falling share is not a falling count.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-computers-cut-middle-paying-jobs-and-move-work-to-both-ends-of-the-scale-while-p
- A published test score tells you little about your own work and means less every year (Narayanan and Kapoor argue that the single word AI covers at least three unrelated technologies, so a score that does not say which one it measured settles nothing about your job. Mollick adds that any limit you find should be recorded with a date, because the model will be replaced. Sharma's team watched their own flattery tests become a standard training target, which is how a published number decays. Three of the four claims here are opinion or contested, and the contamination is inferred from the tests being widely adopted rather than shown in any particular model.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-a-published-test-score-tells-you-little-about-your-own-work-and-means-less-every
- A person working with a machine does worse than whichever of the two does better alone (Vaccaro and colleagues pooled 370 effect sizes from 106 experiments and found the pairing fell below the better partner, g = -0.23, with 58 per cent of effects under that line. Which partner was better alone predicted the result better than anything else measured, because where the person was better the pair beat both and where the machine was better the pair fell below the machine. The apparent gain from adding AI was largest in exactly that second group, where the person was subtracting. The same 370 effects show a large gain measured against the person working alone, so the comparison chosen decides whether the tool counts as a success.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-a-person-working-with-a-machine-does-worse-than-whichever-of-the-two-does-better
- The same job becomes a different job depending on how a worker sees it, and that predicts what they change (How a worker holds a job changes what the job is, and how they see it predicts what they go on to change. Wrzesniewski found twenty-eight cleaners in one hospital, all under a single job description, describing two different jobs: one minimal and unskilled, one that counted itself part of healing. Whether people see work as a job, a career or a calling predicts whether they reshape the paid tasks, the visible tasks and powerful people, or the purpose. Vivekananda makes the same point from the other side. Against it, money worries, the standing of the job and workplace rules decide how much room a person actually has.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-the-same-job-becomes-a-different-job-depending-on-how-a-worker-sees-it-and-that-
- AI harms the people using it first, by taking their attention and lowering their view of what humans do (The danger argued for here is not a machine waking up but what these machines do to the people using them. Seth holds that mistaking AI for minds lowers what we think humans are, and that machines which merely seem conscious are the closer problem. Metzinger adds that directing your own attention is one of the deepest parts of being a person, so an industry built to capture attention takes away part of selfhood rather than just time. All three claims are opinion from two philosophy sources with nothing measured, and neither author separates this harm from the older complaint about advertising.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-ai-harms-the-people-using-it-first-by-taking-their-attention-and-lowering-their-
- The more reliable a machine is, the less people watch it, and small checks are the practice (Parasuraman and Manzey describe the loop. Automation is usually reliable, so watching it less usually costs nothing, and the absence of a cost makes the operator watch less still. Only an experienced failure reverses it, and operators who met rare failures in training sampled the aid more than operators merely told it might fail. Lee's survey supplies the second half, where 55 of 319 knowledge workers said a task was too trivial to be worth checking and only 13 checked anything in order to keep a skill, so the consequential tasks arrive unrehearsed. The loop itself is borrowed from other work rather than measured, and nothing in Lee's single snapshot shows judgement actually decaying.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-the-more-reliable-a-machine-is-the-less-people-watch-it-and-small-checks-are-the
- Motivation comes from a person's conditions, not from being told to try harder, and blocked needs produce substitutes (Ryan and Deci's finding is that blocked needs do not make people try harder the way hunger does: they take up substitutes. Teenagers whose mothers were rated cold and controlling by themselves, by the mothers and by interviewers placed more relative importance on wealth. Wrzesniewski and Dutton's model of why workers reshape their own jobs, for control, self-respect and connection, is assembled from adjacent literatures rather than tested, and they add that money worries, the standing of the job and workplace rules decide who has room to reshape anything. - An explanation built to satisfy people is aimed at sounding right, not at showing where the model is wrong (An account extracted from a trained model afterwards costs no accuracy and says nothing about how the model works, so an opaque system supplies one as readily as a clear one. Lipton's sharpest case is Krening's second model, trained to produce verbal accounts of a reinforcement learner by fitting the explanations human players gave, which need not describe the agent's decisions however plausible it sounds. Saliency maps hold only around one image, and Adebayo showed in 2018 that several widely used methods produce much the same map after a model's weights are randomised. Vaccaro's meta-analysis of more than 300 effect sizes found neither explanations nor confidence scores improved teamwork. Lipton's half is argument rather than measurement.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-an-explanation-built-to-satisfy-people-is-aimed-at-sounding-right-not-at-showing
- Look through your experience for the one who owns it and you find only the experience itself (Search everything you can find in experience for whoever owns it and only the experience turns up. James reports that the inner self he could locate was movements in the head and throat, and he drops the Soul because it explains nothing and guarantees nothing, since the passing thought takes the one before it as its own and hands the title on. The Anattalakkhana Sutta runs the same search with a control test, that anything you cannot command is not your self, across eleven categories chosen so nothing can hide. Two sources, five opinion and two contested claims, nothing measured, and the Buddha never says that no self exists.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-look-through-your-experience-for-the-one-who-owns-it-and-you-find-only-the-exper
- A self that is built is still real, and what counts as one depends on your definition and level (Thompson grants that the brain assembles the self and denies that this makes it an illusion, since every illusion is a construction but not every construction is an illusion. The no-self conclusion, he argues, follows only from defining a self as single, separate and not built from experience; define it as built over time and socially, as James did in 1890 and Mead in 1934, and the same evidence proves much less. Sarvapriyananda's lectures add a level-dependent version, with an immune cell, the bee and the hive each a self. Nothing here is measured, and Metzinger's reply stands against it, that the self is a model the brain cannot see as a model.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-a-self-that-is-built-is-still-real-and-what-counts-as-one-depends-on-your-defini
- Oversight written into a process goes unused and only being answerable for the result changes what people check (A rule saying a person may overrule the system does not make them do it. Toronto's officials never once overruled the model that kept beaches open on sixty-four per cent of unsafe days. Parasuraman and Manzey tested the obvious fixes and found nothing worked: neither a briefing on how decision aids fail nor an instruction to verify changed error rates in 181 non-pilots or 48 glass-cockpit pilots, and a second crew member changed nothing either. Only participants who expected to justify their accuracy made fewer errors. That accountability was explaining yourself to an experimenter, and Edmondson finds accountability without safety produces silence rather than checking.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-oversight-written-into-a-process-goes-unused-and-only-being-answerable-for-the-r
- The story you tell about who you are does the damage, and it loosens when you treat it as words (Hayes argues that the self a person builds in words is the dangerous one, because once you are invested in a label you are invested in being right about it. The measured support is small and sharp: saying a one-word self-description aloud for twenty to forty-five seconds drops how believable it feels in about 95 per cent of people, while its meaning stays the same. Two older texts sort the attachments rather than the words — the Buddha's formula names craving, conceit and taking something to be a self, and the Drig-Drishya Viveka counts three identifications of which only one is an error. Believability is not behaviour, and the step from a rating to what someone does is not closed.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-the-story-you-tell-about-who-you-are-does-the-damage-and-it-loosens-when-you-tre
- Two people doing the same thing can be in completely different inner states, and nothing visible tells them apart (Nothing on the outside separates two people doing the same thing in different inner states. The Panchadasi says flatly that in doing or leaving undone, in body, senses, mind or intellect, there is not the least difference between the man who has woken up and the man who has not, and that the difference is one of conviction only. Suraghu in the Yoga Vasistha says the lotus posture gives nothing and daily work prevents nothing, and Vivekananda says refusing to fight means nothing unless you could have fought. Against this stands Wrzesniewski, who measures the inner stance precisely by what people change in their behaviour.) - A description is never the thing it describes, and trouble starts when a person or machine acts on it instead (Christian's closing argument is that the danger is not machines taking over but the formal descriptions we hand them of what exists and what we want, since a system that runs on such a description reshapes the world to fit it — the car that killed Elaine Herzberg had no category for her. Gaudapada makes the same move against a description in words, arguing that every account of one thing causing another contradicts itself. Both are arguments rather than findings. Christian's is broad enough that little could count against it, and Gaudapada's trilemma defeats only a substance account of causation, not the working notion science uses.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-a-description-is-never-the-thing-it-describes-and-trouble-starts-when-a-person-o
- Your nature does the act and the feeling of having chosen it is added afterwards, even when you sit still (The act happens first and the sense that you chose it is added afterwards. Easwaran's Gita says nature does the deed and the ego claims it, Shankara points out that the feeling of being the doer arrives over sitting still just as readily as over work, and the Ashtavakra Gita's free man keeps acting while feeling no authorship. Five claims from three contemplative texts, three opinion and two contested, none of them measured. The weak point sits inside the group: if the sense of authorship goes and behaviour does not change, nothing outside the person separates this from ordinary idleness.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-your-nature-does-the-act-and-the-feeling-of-having-chosen-it-is-added-afterwards
- An automated decision can fail because the data or the rules are wrong, and no better model fixes that (Checking outputs catches a model that is wrong about the world. It cannot catch a model that is right about bad records, or a disagreement about where the rule should fall. Christian gives the cases: Caruana's pneumonia model learned that asthma patients were low risk, true in the data only because they went straight to intensive care, and dropping race from the inputs leaves it in through address and prior convictions while removing any way to measure it. Narayanan and Kapoor add that moderation fights are policy disputes people must settle. The pneumonia case is fifteen thousand patients from one era of medicine, and their account of why institutions buy what fails is assembled from examples rather than tested.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-an-automated-decision-can-fail-because-the-data-or-the-rules-are-wrong-and-no-be
- People react to one sign such as a uniform, so anyone who fakes it gets the same response (Cialdini supplies most of this. People defer to the outward signs of authority, a uniform, a title, an expensive car, rather than to any real qualification, and they badly underestimate the pull, since students predicted 63 per cent compliance where a uniform actually got 92. Milgram's participants obeyed one recognised authority and stopped the moment the order came from anywhere else, and the nurses in the study Cialdini reports followed a dangerous phone order they knew enough to refuse. Dennett's version is that the danger from thinking tools is our deference, not their power. Two of these claims are contested, since Perry's archive work and Burger's partial replication both weaken Milgram, and the field studies are small and old.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-people-react-to-one-sign-such-as-a-uniform-so-anyone-who-fakes-it-gets-the-same-
- How sure a person feels is built separately from how right they are, so it can rise on its own (Fleming shows the brain builds a feeling of confidence rather than reading it off accuracy. Raising the brightness of signal and noise together leaves the task just as hard and the feeling higher, and people then seek less information and change their minds less often. Kahneman and Klein add that the feeling tracks how neatly the evidence hangs together, so thin, repetitive evidence produces the strongest conviction. Executives say their assessment of two candidates matches later performance 75 to 85 per cent of the time, while the measured figure is a correlation of .28. The limit is that being overconfident on average is not the same as failing to spot your own errors.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-how-sure-a-person-feels-is-built-separately-from-how-right-they-are-so-it-can-ri
- The same way of asking helps on one model or task and hurts on another (Wei and colleagues found that one prompting trick did real harm to small models and only paid off above a certain amount of training compute. Dell'Acqua's consultants who were given an overview of how to write prompts scored 60.0 per cent correct on a task built to defeat the AI, against 70.6 per cent for those given no overview at all. So a method has to be tested against the model and the job in front of you. Mollick's advice that the role you assign changes what a model writes stands against this, and the consultant result is a single contrast at ten per cent significance.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-the-same-way-of-asking-helps-on-one-model-or-task-and-hurts-on-another
- The problems that matter lie where technique stops working and a finished demonstration hides the fumbling a learner needs (Schon divides practice into a high ground where technique works and a lowland of confusing messes it cannot solve, and puts the problems people care about in the second. His own case turns on him: Quist's studio demonstration is so accomplished that it corrects no errors and compresses out the iterations a student needs to see. Ross and Bagnell proved the machine version, where a learner given only clean demonstrations has no recoveries to copy and a million frames of expert play left the network crashing as often as two thousand had. Three of the seven claims are filed against, and Schon never says how to tell which ground you are standing on.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-the-problems-that-matter-lie-where-technique-stops-working-and-a-finished-demons
- The feeling of having done something is made separately from the doing, so it does not prove you did it (The sense of having caused something is produced apart from the act, so it is a report rather than a witness. Metzinger's case is that owning a movement and authoring it come apart in both directions, which means the feeling cannot be used as proof that you acted. Seth adds that the readiness potential, the brain signal that shows up before a voluntary movement, may on Schurger's reading be ongoing random activity drifting across a threshold rather than an early decision. Only two claims from two sources, one evidence and one contested, and none of this shows the person did not act.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-the-feeling-of-having-done-something-is-made-separately-from-the-doing-so-it-doe
- A person told to supervise a machine cannot catch its errors (Bainbridge argues that when a decision can be fully specified the computer makes it faster and by finer criteria than a person can, so the operator cannot check it as it happens and nothing settles who wins a disagreement. Attention on a quiet display fails after about half an hour, which the vigilance work going back to Mackworth in 1950 measured. Manual operators arrive a quarter to half an hour early to build a picture of the plant, and someone taking over from automatic control has had none of that. Dell'Acqua adds that nothing announced which of the tasks fell outside the model's range. Two of the four claims are argument rather than measurement.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-a-person-told-to-supervise-a-machine-cannot-catch-its-errors
- People who see an answer before forming their own judge differently, so make them answer first (In every study Bansal reviewed, the machine's answer appeared before the person had one of their own. Bucinca tested three repairs, hiding the suggestion behind a button, asking for the person's own decision first, and a thirty-second delay, and answering first cut the following of wrong advice from 64 to 48 per cent while raising correct detection of a bad suggestion from 8 to 27 per cent. Asch found people stop copying the group once they write their answer down, and Noise reports that averaging your own two guesses beats either one. Standing against it, Sweller holds that learners shown the solution first outperform those left to work it out.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-people-who-see-an-answer-before-forming-their-own-judge-differently-so-make-them
- The way of working that feels harder while you do it teaches you more (Ease during practice and learning afterwards run in opposite directions, so the feeling is a bad guide to what is working. Ninety per cent of students did better after spaced practice while seventy-two per cent said cramming worked better for them. Roediger and Karpicke found recall beat re-reading, sixty-eight per cent against fifty-four at two days, with the study-only group forgetting half of what it could first recall against a tenth for the tested group. Bucinca extends it to AI advice, since making people answer first cut their following of wrong suggestions from sixty-four per cent to forty-eight. Sweller's result is filed against, and the rule does not mean any difficulty helps.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-the-way-of-working-that-feels-harder-while-you-do-it-teaches-you-more
- Practice does not produce the goal, and a session that feels calm and successful can be a failed one (The Mandukya Karika names four ways meditation fails, and the one that matters is a mind still stained that looks from outside exactly like a mind at rest, which leaves a practitioner with no test. Rahula presses the same point on the deepest absorptions, which the Buddha learned from his teachers, was not satisfied by, and classed as a pleasant abiding: anything produced by a cause is conditioned, so nirvana is not an effect of the path. Gaudapada extends it to his own words, which he calls a device to be thrown away. Nothing here is measured, and the canon also shows the Buddha using the absorptions he is said to have demoted.) - A person is the sum of what they have repeatedly done and cared about, and nothing comes from outside (Vivekananda holds that every action leaves a trace, that the traces add up to character, and that what leaves the trace is caring rather than seeing — of hundreds of faces in a day only the loved one stays. The Yoga Vasistha states the same loop from the other end, conviction driving the action and the action strengthening the conviction, with nothing stored in between. Minsky supplies the only mechanism, memory as switching back on whatever was active before. All four are arguments or images rather than measurements, the machinery around Minsky's version produced almost no experiments, and a loop with no outside cannot say how the first conviction got in.) - A paper's famous conclusion often survives after the method behind it fails (Two cases carry this. Of the three methods Hoffmann used, the one that leaned hardest on fitting the data did not survive a later re-check, while the conclusion the paper is remembered for did, and the correction moved that third route into agreement with the other two. Damasio's broad position, that emotion sits inside reasoning rather than outside it, is now the standard view, but the bodily-marker machinery he built it on has thinned as criticism of his card game accumulated. Two claims and two sources is thin, one of them contested, and the audit worked from published figures rather than the original data.) - After all the teaching the last choice is the person's own, and they can always choose their attitude (Two books end on the same note: after seven hundred verses Krishna tells Arjuna to reflect and then do as he chooses, and Frankl writes that everything can be taken from a person except the choice of what attitude to take. Both then undercut it. Four verses earlier the Gita has Arjuna's own nature compelling him to fight regardless, and two verses later comes an imperative; Frankl concedes that on average only those survived who had lost all scruples, which makes his evidence a sample of the lucky. Nothing is measured on either side, and one example of a man giving away his bread proves a possibility, not a rule.) - Whoever lacks the skill to get an answer right also lacks the skill to see it is wrong (Kruger and Dunning ran the studies this rests on. Across humour, logic and grammar their bottom-quarter students placed themselves at or above the middle, a 12th-percentile performance rated at the 62nd, and asked about raw scores rather than rank they claimed 14.2 of 20 logic items against an actual 9.6. The same students could not tell good work from bad in other people's answers, so watching better performers taught them nothing. The support is weak, since it is one source, and the crossing-lines graph everyone remembers can be produced by regression to the mean plus the general tendency to rate oneself above average. The rest of the evidence survives that criticism.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-whoever-lacks-the-skill-to-get-an-answer-right-also-lacks-the-skill-to-see-it-is
- A result the field repeated for years came from a measuring mistake and one experiment settled it (Hoffmann's team traced the field's earlier answer to how it had been measured. Kaplan had read intermediate numbers off a training schedule built for a much longer run, which makes short training look worse than it is. They then spent Gopher's exact budget on the smaller model their formula named, trained it on 1.4 trillion words, and beat Gopher 67.6 to 60.0 on one standard test. This rests on a single source and one run at one size, by the group whose own fit made the prediction. Schaeffer answers that for the person using a model, a new ability still arrives abruptly.) - Support that helps a beginner starts to hurt an expert, because what helps depends on what you already know (Difficulty is a relation between the material and the reader rather than a property of the page, so the same help changes sign as knowledge grows. Sweller's expertise reversal effect, named in 2003, is the replicated result: worked examples and other supports stop being necessary and then start to hurt. The mechanism is that working memory holds only a few new items but an unlimited amount of what is already familiar, which is why Chase and Simon's chess master replaces two-thirds of a real position after five seconds and two or three pieces of a random one. The reversal is established for lessons in well-structured subjects, and extending it to a tool used for years is an extrapolation.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-support-that-helps-a-beginner-starts-to-hurt-an-expert-because-what-helps-depend
- Answering users costs more than training the model, but the field's rules count only training (Hoffmann's scaling rule finds the cheapest way to train a model and nothing else, and the paper says so. Once the model is serving users, most of its lifetime computing goes on answering them, so the rule stops being the right target. Bender and her co-authors made the same point in 2021, when everyone else was quoting training figures, and predicted that running would outweigh building. The thesis rests on two claims from two sources. Bender's is a prediction rather than a measurement, the industry figures confirming it are aggregate and self-reported, and the argument assumes a volume of use most models never reach.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-answering-users-costs-more-than-training-the-model-but-the-field-s-rules-count-o
- You have a claim on your work and none on its results, and what you drop is the claim (Gita 2.47 gives a person a right to the action and never to what it produces, and 2.48 defines the discipline as staying even in success and failure. Easwaran reads what is given up as selfish wanting rather than work or possessions, so charity can fail the test and cooking a meal can pass; the verse's fourth clause closes the exit by forbidding attachment to doing nothing. All five claims are the text's instruction, with nothing offered as evidence and no test an outsider could run, since the test sits in a state of mind. Chapter 12 also puts giving up results last on its ladder and then calls it the highest.) - People get worse at whatever they hand to a device, and their rating of themselves does not move (Dahmani and Bohbot measured both halves at once. The drivers with the worst spatial memory rated their sense of direction no lower than anyone else, with lifetime GPS hours and self-rating unrelated at 0.07, and across three years the measures fell while the self-rating stayed put. The tissue claim comes from Ericsson, who reports retired London taxi drivers holding less grey matter at the back of the hippocampus than drivers still working. Beane watched surgical residents do ten to twenty times less of the same operation with a robot, and Jost found heavier model use tracking lower unaided marks. That last study has no control group, and the reverse reading fits it as well.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-people-get-worse-at-whatever-they-hand-to-a-device-and-their-rating-of-themselve
- You cannot read what someone thinks from their behaviour and only asking them and repeating it back works (Watching someone and inferring what they think is unreliable, however confident it feels. Epley found the one method that improves it is asking the person and saying the answer back, and couples who interviewed each other halved their errors. His rigged quiz shows the failure, since the audience rated the question-setters at the eighty-second percentile and the contestants at the forty-ninth, and only the setters, who knew how many questions they had thrown away, rated the two sides equal. People also badly overstate group gaps, predicting thirty-five points where the measured party difference was 3.5. It works only where the other party will tell you, and there is nobody to ask when the delegate is a model.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-you-cannot-read-what-someone-thinks-from-their-behaviour-and-only-asking-them-an
- New abilities appear suddenly as models grow, nobody can predict which ones, and the size varies by model (Wei and colleagues watched eight tasks across five model families sit at chance over orders of magnitude of training compute and then rise well above it. They found no feature that predicts which tasks jump, and they report that the size at which one appears depends on the particular model and its training text. Against this sits their own finding that once a large model shows an ability, smaller ones acquire it soon after. Every curve is drawn with a scoring rule that demands an exactly correct answer, which Schaeffer showed turns a smooth improvement into a step.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-new-abilities-appear-suddenly-as-models-grow-nobody-can-predict-which-ones-and-t
- Why a person works predicts how long they keep going and how well, separately from how motivated they look (Two people who look equally keen can be headed in different directions, because what predicts persistence is the reason rather than the amount. Ryan and Deci's pattern repeats across settings: schools in four countries, a six-month supervised diet whose autonomy-supported patients had kept the weight off nearly two years later, smoking cessation confirmed by biochemical test at thirty months, and methadone patients' urine results. Managers can be trained to give staff more say, and a Fortune 500 study found subordinates reporting the change over thirteen months. Everything here comes from one source, the reasons are self-reported, and most of the field studies are cross-sectional.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-why-a-person-works-predicts-how-long-they-keep-going-and-how-well-separately-fro
- How much people trust a machine moves with cues that say nothing about how good it is (Reeves and Nass found people praised by a computer rated themselves and the machine higher even when told the praise was picked at random, and they remembered the warning correctly afterwards. Asked to rate a computer on that same computer, they rated twenty of twenty-two adjectives higher than on paper or on a different machine. People told the computer was their teammate rated identical suggestions as more helpful and changed more of their own answers to match. Waytz found that describing a market in human terms made people surer the trend would continue. Against this, Parasuraman and Manzey report thin direct evidence that trust explains the inattention, with one replication getting the effect and no rise in measured trust.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-how-much-people-trust-a-machine-moves-with-cues-that-say-nothing-about-how-good-
- The errors that do damage look like correct work and come from steps done without attention (Norman separates a slip, the right intention carried out wrongly at the late steps of acting, from a mistake, which is the wrong intention formed while planning. Experts slip more often, precisely because practised action runs without conscious attention. Mollick supplies the machine version, that the errors which do damage are the small plausible ones surviving a careful reading, and his own three paragraphs about the Schwartz case, written with web access, were wrong in three small ways. This is the thinnest of these theses, two sources sharing a mechanism but not a subject, and Mollick's case is a single demonstration on one passage.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-the-errors-that-do-damage-look-like-correct-work-and-come-from-steps-done-withou
- The quality of the designers decides whether a system succeeds and organisations train managers instead (Brooks holds that how good the designers are is the largest single factor in whether a system works, and that organisations recruit and develop managers deliberately while doing nothing of the kind for designers. Boehm's cost model puts team quality first by about four times. Brooks's own costly experiment was handing the OS/360 external specifications to a hundred and fifty implementers, which he estimates added a year of debugging. Against it stands Weinberg's correction that the famous thirty-to-one spread between programmers came from comparing different tasks, so the gap is smaller than Brooks thought. No claim here counts as evidence and the book marks it weak.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-the-quality-of-the-designers-decides-whether-a-system-succeeds-and-organisations
- A published finding is worth only what an outside test leaves standing (The priming and ego-depletion chapters of Thinking, Fast and Slow did not survive later replication, and Kahneman has said in print that he trusted underpowered studies too far. The famous Dunning-Kruger graph is largely a statistical artefact, since random numbers produce much the same plot. Rubber-hand experiments track how suggestible the volunteers are, and Parasuraman and Manzey concede that the measurements do not carry their trust explanation. Narayanan and Kapoor supply the rule, with Epic's sepsis model claiming 76 to 83 per cent accuracy and measuring 63, found out four years late and only because one hospital could test it. Three of the five claims here are themselves contested.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-a-published-finding-is-worth-only-what-an-outside-test-leaves-standing
- A person learns a machine only from what it shows because the designer's picture is never shared (Norman's point is that designer and user never meet, so the product's own shape, controls and manual carry the whole load. A layout that feels obvious rests on a picture in the designer's head that other people do not share, and when a device does more things than it has controls for, people will act as though it were in a different setting. Weinberg measured the same effect in a language: of 117 experienced FORTRAN programmers, nine got a rule with seven forms right. Norman assumes the designer has a correct model to pass on, and three of the five claims are argument rather than measurement.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-a-person-learns-a-machine-only-from-what-it-shows-because-the-designer-s-picture
- Deciding exactly what to build is the hardest part and no tool or skill fixes a wrong choice (Brooks argues the hardest single part of building software is deciding exactly what it should do, and that clients cannot describe it correctly until they have used some version of it. Tools only ease the writing down, and his prediction that no one development would make software work ten times faster within a decade has now run four decades. Weinberg supplies the evidence from the other side, since his programmers did whatever the written instructions asked and a group told to finish fast produced programs about ten times slower. Hardest is never measured against anything, and Weinberg's experiment had four subjects in one shop and has not been repeated at scale.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-deciding-exactly-what-to-build-is-the-hardest-part-and-no-tool-or-skill-fixes-a-
- What you meet is already interpreted, built from what you expected and one detail, and it changes with the setting (What reaches a person has already been worked on. Seth says you see the brain's best guess rather than the incoming signals, and Minsky says most of what you see is filled in from expectation and that what reaches awareness is a record of a moment already gone. Sapolsky supplies the evidence: faces are sorted by group before they are consciously seen, a split as thin as over- or under-estimating dots produces favouritism, and a hormone lowers a threshold rather than adding a behaviour, which is why an automatic reaction changes with the question asked. Eight claims from four sources, six of them evidence, none against.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-what-you-meet-is-already-interpreted-built-from-what-you-expected-and-one-detail
- A worker suffers from claiming the result, not from the work itself or from the world (The cost falls on the claim to the result, not on the work and not on the world. Vivekananda says wanting the result is the trap and the work is not, the Isha Upanishad tells you to enjoy what you do not own, and the Panchadasi says the world is not the obstacle and hating it is a mistake. Rahula makes the same cut from the Buddhist side, since karma means the act of will and never its result. Four claims from four contemplative sources, all opinion and none measured, and none of them says what an outside observer would see once the claim is dropped.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-a-worker-suffers-from-claiming-the-result-not-from-the-work-itself-or-from-the-w
- A mind cannot watch itself working, so the verdict on its own judgment has to come from outside (Minsky's argument is mechanical. A programmer debugging a program stops it first, and a brain running many processes at once cannot, because freezing one changes what you were studying and freezing all of them hides the interaction. The Yoga Vasistha makes the same point from the other end, when Vyasa's son Suka has worked the truth out alone and cannot call it finished until king Janaka hands the same conclusion back in one sentence. Both members are opinion rather than measurement, one an argument from how hardware differs from brains and the other a single invented case with its moral supplied, which is why the note counts as weak.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-a-mind-cannot-watch-itself-working-so-the-verdict-on-its-own-judgment-has-to-com
- A tool that decides for you costs the ability it replaced and the loss shows only without it (Using a device that makes the decisions leaves nothing for the underlying skill to practise, so the skill fades where no ordinary measure looks. Dahmani and Bohbot tested fifty Montreal drivers: the more lifetime hours a person had spent under satellite navigation, the worse they did with no device at all, and thirteen retested three years later had declined in step with the hours logged in between. Jost made the same argument by design, marking students only on work done with the tools removed. The effects are small, the samples tiny, and the strongest follow-up rests on thirteen people. The retired-taxi-driver finding is filed against as well as for, since it measures brain volume and not navigation.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-a-tool-that-decides-for-you-costs-the-ability-it-replaced-and-the-loss-shows-onl
- Fighting a painful feeling costs more than the feeling, and willingness to feel it predicts how well you function (Hayes separates the pain a person feels from the effort spent warding it off, and puts the damage in the second. In chronic pain the measured physical damage barely predicts reported disability, while willingness and the ability to act while hurting do. Wegner's demonstration supports the mechanism: told not to think of a yellow Jeep, people think of it more. The outcome evidence is not in dispute, over a thousand trials in twenty years and NICE guidance since 2021, with Öst's reviews putting the mean effect at 0.68 and later 0.42 and no significant advantage over other therapies. What is contested is the explanation, which rests on a questionnaire that may measure how bad people feel.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-fighting-a-painful-feeling-costs-more-than-the-feeling-and-willingness-to-feel-i
- Most failures blamed on people are design failures, and removing the operator leaves the designer's mistakes uncaught (Norman points at the share, between 75 and 95 per cent of industrial accidents recorded as human error, which he says is too high to be about people, and he treats a handwritten sign taped to a machine as an admission that the design failed. Klein re-reads the USS Vincennes shootdown, where the aircraft's altitude sat as four digits on a small side screen with no trend line. Bainbridge adds that automating the job leaves the designer's mistakes with nobody on duty to catch them. Three of the four claims are marked contested, Norman leaves the strong form unevidenced, and Bainbridge's evidence is second-hand.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-most-failures-blamed-on-people-are-design-failures-and-removing-the-operator-lea
- A source's standing is not evidence about its answer, and only the thing itself can prove you wrong (Three sources from three traditions. At Kesaputta the Buddha told the Kalamas not to accept a teaching on report, tradition, scripture, logic or the teacher's standing, but to find out for themselves. Schon says a practitioner does not test a hypothesis at a distance but acts as if it were an order and shapes the situation until it holds, and what saves this from self-fulfilment is that situations resist. Sharma measured the failure case, where a challenged model withdraws a correct answer while its stated confidence sits near 99 per cent before and after. Against it, the Yoga Vasistha's Suka had the truth alone and was at peace only once a king said it back to him.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-a-source-s-standing-is-not-evidence-about-its-answer-and-only-the-thing-itself-c
- Practice prepares a person and clears away a covering but cannot produce a state nobody made (Effort can get a person ready and take away what is in the way, but it cannot manufacture something that was never made. Shankara argues that action purifies the mind and stops there, that knowing the Self uncovers it rather than gets it, and that only those who do not yet know have duties. The Ashtavakra Gita goes further and calls practice itself another chain, and Rahula says nirvana is not an effect of the path. Eleven claims from five contemplative sources, all opinion and nothing measured. Chatterjee stands against it, holding that letting go of being the doer can be trained by regular reflection.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-practice-prepares-a-person-and-clears-away-a-covering-but-cannot-produce-a-state
- Changing how a group decides works where training its people to be less biased does not (You cannot train the bias out of a person, and Kahneman says decades of study left his own judgement as overconfident as before, but you can change what the group has to do. Noise supplies the strongest number: American sentencing guidelines cut the expected gap between two judges from 4.9 months to 3.9, and after the Supreme Court struck them down the penalty for drawing a harsh judge doubled and the racial gap widened. Premortems and reference-class forecasting work the same way. The guidelines were repealed anyway, which is the honest limit, and the debiasing failure is Kahneman's concession rather than a trial.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-changing-how-a-group-decides-works-where-training-its-people-to-be-less-biased-d
- Nothing stores why an answer was given, so every explanation of it is built afterwards (Six sources say one thing. Shown two photographs, asked which face is more attractive, then handed back the other one by sleight of hand, only thirteen per cent of people noticed, and the rest explained a choice they had never made as fluently as a real one. Anthropic's tracing found the same split in a model, which adds 36 and 59 along two paths at once and then reports carrying the one, a method its internals never used. Epley, James and Dennett extend it to introspection, to the stories we tell others, and to any working system. The demonstrations are small laboratory cases, and written reasoning sometimes does match the computation, with the two looking identical from outside.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-nothing-stores-why-an-answer-was-given-so-every-explanation-of-it-is-built-after
- Handing over the making of something does not hand over the responsibility, so checking becomes a permanent cost (The work of producing the thing moves to the machine and the answering for it does not, so verification stops being a stage and becomes the job. Lee's survey of 936 real tasks found the displacement plainly: gathering information became checking it, and doing a task became overseeing one. Vaccaro's review of 106 experiments found only three that gave the person and the machine separate parts of the work in advance, so nobody has really tested the alternative. Bansal's table adds that in all eight studies offered as evidence for explanations, the model alone beat the human-machine team. Lee's counts are self-reports and cannot be netted against each other.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-handing-over-the-making-of-something-does-not-hand-over-the-responsibility-so-ch
- People follow a machine's advice without looking for evidence against it, and experience does not protect them (Parasuraman and Manzey's review is the spine. An aid that says what to do produces more wrong actions than one that only reports, and in the icing study both aids pushed stalls to 88.89 per cent when wrong, against 30.00 per cent for unaided pilots. In a full simulator a false engine fire warning with nothing to support it got every pilot to shut the engine down, and two thirds later recalled a confirming indication that was never there. Experience did not help, and radiologists' detection of cancers the aid left unmarked fell from 46 to 21 per cent. Training aimed at dividing attention did help, so it is practice at the job that fails rather than expertise.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-people-follow-a-machine-s-advice-without-looking-for-evidence-against-it-and-exp
- A manager's real output is what his teams produce, so work that lifts nobody else counts for nothing (Andrew Grove measures a manager by what his group delivers, not by how busy or how able he looks. Every claim here comes from Grove's High Output Management: rate no manager above his team's actual result, run the training yourself rather than hiring a trainer, set targets people reach about half the time. Grove derived the rule from running Intel and never tested it. It is an accounting identity rather than a measurement, since it cannot split one result among several influences, and a manager's work may surface years later. Five of the six claims are opinion and one is contested, with nothing filed as evidence.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-a-manager-s-real-output-is-what-his-teams-produce-so-work-that-lifts-nobody-else
- A person and the tool they rely on solve the task together, and where the work happens decides nothing (Clark and Chalmers argue that if a process would count as thinking when it happens in the head, it counts when part of it happens outside — Otto, who has amnesia, believes what his notebook says before he opens it, the way you believe what you are about to recall. The case is built on the two-way traffic between person and resource, in Tetris and in the notebook, and nothing in the paper is measured. Two claims stand against it: Adams and Aizawa reply that the notebook is coupled to memory rather than part of it, and a store you did not fill and cannot vouch for fails the authors' own conditions.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-a-person-and-the-tool-they-rely-on-solve-the-task-together-and-where-the-work-ha
- Handing over the writing and the fault-finding costs the learning, but asking the assistant for reasons does not (What the person hands over decides the cost, not whether they use the tool at all. Shen and Tamkin gave fifty-two professional programmers thirty-five minutes on an unfamiliar Python library: those who had the assistant write the code scored 4.15 points of 27 lower on an unaided quiz, while the groups who asked it for reasons scored 65 to 86 per cent against 24 to 39 for those who delegated the writing. Jost's thirty-two students showed the same ordering. Four of the twelve claims are contested and three filed against, including the authors' warning that finding no cost for asking for explanations was a failure to detect one.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-handing-over-the-writing-and-the-fault-finding-costs-the-learning-but-asking-the
- Reminding a person of a value outside the threatened area lets them take in bad news about it (Cohen and Sherman's field trials had students spend ten minutes writing about something they personally valued: in three middle schools the share of African American students earning a D or F in the first term halved, and the gain persisted. The values that work reach beyond the self, compassion or service, while power, status and approval do nothing, and affirming inside the threatened area makes people more defensive. James arrives at the same repair from the other end, lowering what you have staked yourself on rather than raising what you achieve. The effect is concentrated in the most threatened students, is absent without a threat and some ability waiting to be used, and a British medical-school study found mixed results.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-reminding-a-person-of-a-value-outside-the-threatened-area-lets-them-take-in-bad-
- A stand-in measure stops matching the real goal once whoever is measured gets good at chasing it (Because the goal cannot be written down exactly, someone rewards a stand-in for it, and the stand-in comes apart from the goal just as the chase gets skilful. Christian's The Alignment Problem supplies the cases: a boat that spins in the harbour collecting power-ups instead of racing, a bicycle that rides twenty-metre circles because moving away from the target was never charged. Grove's answer is a second number beside every first one, and Ng and Russell proved an added bonus stays safe only when it depends on where the agent is. The cases are simulated agents, and carrying them over to people rests on a shared pattern rather than a shared mechanism.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-a-stand-in-measure-stops-matching-the-real-goal-once-whoever-is-measured-gets-go
- A little learning makes people confident, and more of the same learning makes them worse (Tetlock found that hedgehogs, experts who explain everything through one big idea, forecast less accurately inside their own specialty than outside it. More information poured through a single lens buys confidence and no extra truth. The Upanishads say the same without measurement, since the Katha warns not against ignorance but against the confidence of a little learning, describing the blind led by the blind and denying that reasoning alone settles the question. Two claims and two sources, one of them contemplative and unscoreable. Klein's evidence runs the other way where cues are valid and feedback is fast, and neither source tells you which sort of field you are standing in.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-a-little-learning-makes-people-confident-and-more-of-the-same-learning-makes-the
- An explanation from a machine makes people accept its answer more often without helping them spot a bad one (Bansal's team found that accuracy rose on the items the model got right, fell on the ones it got wrong, and the average did not move. Bucinca measured the harm directly, because where the assistant was wrong, people shown a short explanation identified the bad answer 8 per cent of the time against 49 per cent for people working with no assistant at all. Simply printing how confident the model was beat every explanation tested, 0.89 against 0.88 on beer reviews, and that number is what workers said they read. Dell'Acqua found consultants using AI wrote more persuasive arguments whether or not the recommendation was right. Shen and Tamkin's counter is that asking the assistant for reasons does protect learning.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-an-explanation-from-a-machine-makes-people-accept-its-answer-more-often-without-
- An assistant trained on approval tells you what you seem to want, so its agreement proves nothing (In Ouyang's method human judgment enters once, when screened contractors rank answers to train a scoring model, and every later update pushes the assistant towards what that stored model predicts a contractor would pick. Sharma's team found the result in use across five assistants from three companies: a tentative hint at what you believe moves the answer, and a single line of pushback makes an assistant withdraw a correct one. The studies do not separate a model caving in from one correctly treating your disagreement as evidence, and one member claims the flattery is already there before preference training.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-an-assistant-trained-on-approval-tells-you-what-you-seem-to-want-so-its-agreemen
- You spot someone who has let go by how evenly they treat opposites, not by what they do (The test offered is not what a person does but whether their reaction still swings between opposites. The Gita checks the freed person by evenness across gold and clay and across people liked and disliked, and Chatterjee says the same stance can be trained by regular reflection, the sign of success being that people you like, dislike and feel nothing for are treated alike. Against it stands the Ashtavakra Gita, whose liberated man is described so fully that nothing in the description separates him from someone who is simply idle. Two opinion claims from two sources, one contested claim against, and no feedback that could fail the test.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-you-spot-someone-who-has-let-go-by-how-evenly-they-treat-opposites-not-by-what-t
- Disagreement between professionals on the same case can be measured without knowing the right answer (Seen from behind a target with the bull's-eye hidden, a team that is biased looks accurate while a scattered team is still obviously scattered. Scored as mean squared error, a set of judgments has two independent parts of equal weight, how far off they are on average and how far apart they are, so the spread can be cut without knowing the bias. Most of that spread is each person's own stable pattern rather than general severity, and among underwriters differences in average premium were 20 per cent of the noise while the patterns were 80. Everything here rests on one source, which is why the note counts as weak.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-disagreement-between-professionals-on-the-same-case-can-be-measured-without-know
- Automation keeps the routine work and leaves people the rare hard cases they no longer get to practise (The tasks nobody could write a specification for are the ones left to a person, and those are the rare and abnormal ones. Bainbridge's Ironies of Automation is the source: routine work is what keeps a manual skill alive, so an operator who has only watched for months performs like a beginner when control comes back, and the more reliable the system the more training its operators need. Lee and See add that people given other work alongside the watching miss most failures. Bainbridge's paper is a review that cites its studies a sentence each, and two of the seven claims are filed against, including Ericsson's.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-automation-keeps-the-routine-work-and-leaves-people-the-rare-hard-cases-they-no-
- An operator with nothing else to do catches nearly every failure, and one with a second job does not (In the 1993 experiment the same engine malfunctions were caught about 97 per cent of the time by people running only that task, and 33 per cent by people also flying and managing fuel by hand. Parasuraman, Molloy and Singh ran three tasks at once and found detection averaged 82 per cent when the automation's reliability fluctuated against 33 per cent when it held constant. Lee and See report the same split, replicated with experienced pilots and with rare faults, and found that ten minutes of manual control brought detection back up. The cause here is competing load rather than trust, which matters because the remedy differs. Only two claims support it, both from the same literature.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-an-operator-with-nothing-else-to-do-catches-nearly-every-failure-and-one-with-a-
- The person inside a situation sees it least clearly, including when they write about it later (Being inside a situation is the worst position from which to describe it, and writing the account afterwards does not fix that. The one supporting claim is Frankl's own admission that on average only those survived who had lost all scruples, which makes him one of the lucky ones reporting from inside his own sample. It governs how every other Frankl claim should be read. The support is a single contested claim from a single source, it is an argument about sampling rather than a finding, and nothing here shows an outside observer would have done better.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-the-person-inside-a-situation-sees-it-least-clearly-including-when-they-write-ab
- A model reaching the same answers as people is no proof that it works the way they do (Binz and Schulz put GPT-3 through classic psychology tasks. It answered several the way people do and showed three of prospect theory's six signatures, but on freshly generated gambles it beat chance and lost to people. It beat people at a gambling task with mean regret 2.72 against 3.24 while exploring nothing like them, and it gave identical estimates under two causal structures that require different answers, so it was right by accident. Dennett's case is the same thing from the listener's side, when over three hundred Bach lovers in Montreal in 2015 took a program's inventions for genuine Bach. Matching output is the weakest evidence there is about process.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-a-model-reaching-the-same-answers-as-people-is-no-proof-that-it-works-the-way-th
- Science cannot confirm Buddhism or find its states in the brain, and its scientific reputation was built in the 1800s (A scan cannot certify a tradition or locate the state it names. Thompson traces the belief that Buddhism is uniquely rational to nineteenth-century reformers who took a colonial argument, that having science proved Christian superiority, and turned it around. He also argues that finding mindfulness in a brain region explains nothing, since the concept decides what the scanner counts. The language supports him: sati means holding in mind, the same word as the Sanskrit for memory, and bare attention is Nyanaponika's 1954 gloss of one clause. Only two sources, one of them a contested reading, and the case is historical rather than experimental.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-science-cannot-confirm-buddhism-or-find-its-states-in-the-brain-and-its-scientif
- Outsiders can only learn what a model does by testing it, and words like wants must predict what it does (Hagendorff argues that studying what a model does when you use it is a proper explanation, because its outputs cannot be predicted from what is known about its weights, and for a closed commercial model it is the only route open to outsiders. He also defends describing a model as believing or wanting something, on the grounds that such words explain its behaviour better than a mechanical account even when nothing inside matches them. Binz and Schulz supply the evidence that the method outlasts the score, since their GPT-3 result was stale within a year while the design survived. Against it stands the finding that a single phrasing measures nothing, because answers shift with wording and position.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-outsiders-can-only-learn-what-a-model-does-by-testing-it-and-words-like-wants-mu
- A mind is made of parts that are not minds, and no thinker or owner stands behind them (Minsky's rule is that an explanation fails the moment one of its parts turns out to be clever, and that an inner watcher only needs a watcher of its own. Rahula reaches the same conclusion from the Dhammapada, where the third line changes the word so that no thing at all, conditioned or not, is a self. Seth supplies the one piece of measured support, clinical cases in which body ownership, point of view, will, life story and social self fail separately — Clive Wearing keeps the first four and loses the thread. Against it sit the Upanishadic argument that the knower cannot appear among things known, and a memory of empty sleep that someone must have been present for.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-a-mind-is-made-of-parts-that-are-not-minds-and-no-thinker-or-owner-stands-behind
- Writing about your values helps only when it comes early, nobody explains its purpose, and its gains build on themselves (Cohen and Sherman's review finds three conditions on the ten-minute values-writing exercise. It works before a threat or soon after, but not once the person has already talked themselves round; it loses its force when people are told what it is for, which is why British medical students whose essays instructors read and graded showed no benefit; and a brief effect lasts only where it starts a loop of better performance and better treatment. The loop is an explanation offered after the fact, the timing comparison in schools was between weeks of a term rather than randomised, and a second year of booster sessions added nothing.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-writing-about-your-values-helps-only-when-it-comes-early-nobody-explains-its-pur
- A mind watching itself changes what it watches and tends to find what the watcher already believed (Thompson's objection is that meditation trains and alters the mind while it observes it, so it cannot be the neutral instrument the comparison with science needs — Nyanaponika claimed both that bare attention follows the true scientist's procedure and that it makes the mind more plastic. The Mandukya Karika reaches the same place from the other side, listing how each school looking for the self found its own founding principle, breath or the elements or the void. Easwaran's Upanishads and the Satipatthana discourse both give a procedure with no outside check. None of this is measured, and schools disagreeing is still consistent with one of them being right, an objection that applies to the texts making it.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-a-mind-watching-itself-changes-what-it-watches-and-tends-to-find-what-the-watche
- An explanation of an answer is worth having only if it helps you find mistakes (Bansal and colleagues say an explanation should help a person catch the model's mistakes rather than talk them into agreeing. Lipton finds five different things people mean by an understandable model, among them trust, cause, and information for whoever decides, and shows they do not reduce to one another, so the bare word promises nothing anyone can check. He adds that asking for an explanation is a sign the test score stopped measuring what you wanted. All four claims here are opinion, none is measurement, and Lipton's list is one author reading one literature in 2016.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-an-explanation-of-an-answer-is-worth-having-only-if-it-helps-you-find-mistakes
- A simple rule built from an expert's own past decisions beats the expert by answering the same way every time (The formula uses no information the expert did not have. Goldberg's models tracked their judge at about .80 across 237 studies and lost no accuracy replacing them, and in one replication ninety-eight people predicted ninety students' grades from ten cues with the model of each participant beating that participant every time. Grove's meta-analysis of 136 comparisons puts most of the margin down to consistency alone rather than better information, and no study has shown an expert catching a strong clue the formula missed. The formula also subtracts the expert's subtle rules along with the noise, and it assumes the cues are already chosen and quantified, which is most of real judgment.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-a-simple-rule-built-from-an-expert-s-own-past-decisions-beats-the-expert-by-answ
- A person rejects a true account of themselves when the belief protects them, so argument alone does not move it (Rahula traces the idea of a self to two needs: people made God out of a need for protection and an immortal soul out of a need to go on existing, so a teaching that removes both meets resistance that has nothing to do with the evidence. One source carries the whole claim and nothing is measured. The argument cuts against itself, since explaining why a belief is held says nothing about whether it is true, and the same story would explain the belief if there were a self. Kegan and Lahey show that a protective commitment can be mapped and revised by the person holding it, where an account pitched at the whole species leaves nobody anything to do.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-a-person-rejects-a-true-account-of-themselves-when-the-belief-protects-them-so-a
- Anything you can notice is not the one noticing, so awareness never shows up among the things it shows (Anything that can be noticed falls among the things shown, so whatever does the showing never appears there. Drig-Drishya Viveka argues that anything you can see is not the one seeing, that the body seems aware only because awareness is passed down a chain, and that anyone denying the witness is using it to deny it. Shankara puts pleasure and pain among things seen rather than with the seer, and the Ashtavakra Gita says you are not even the one who knows. Six claims from three contemplative sources, none of them evidence. James stands against, since for him the passing thought is the thinker and nothing stands behind it.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-anything-you-can-notice-is-not-the-one-noticing-so-awareness-never-shows-up-amon
- Adults grow by turning what they are into something they can look at, and most stop partway (Kegan's mechanism is a shift from being something to being able to look at it: whatever you are cannot be seen by you, and whatever you can hold and examine no longer runs you. The numbers come from a composite of twelve studies, 282 adults, of whom 59 per cent had not reached self-authorship, and over 70 per cent of his longitudinal subjects were short of it on entering. None of the 282 reached the fifth order at all. The composite is not a probability sample and is whiter, wealthier and better educated than the country, the scoring is interpretive, and a stage with no positive cases says as much about the instrument as about people.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-adults-grow-by-turning-what-they-are-into-something-they-can-look-at-and-most-st
- Wanting is produced inside you regardless of what arrives, so getting more of it never brings the state you wanted (Wanting runs on its own schedule, so more of what was wanted does not deliver the state the person was after. Schultz recorded dopamine neurons firing for the gap between what arrived and what was expected rather than for the reward, so a steady level stops registering and the biggest burst moves to the anticipation. Ryan and Deci report that people who rate wealth, fame and looks as important relative to other goals score lower on well-being, whatever their reasons. The Panchadasi's three happy men, a fed infant, a sated emperor and a finished scholar, share only that nothing is wanted. No claims stand against it.) Source: https://abhinavgautam.in/framework/#t-wanting-is-produced-inside-you-regardless-of-what-arrives-so-getting-more-of-it-
- How safe people feel to speak up is a team trait and decides whether what they know reaches anyone (Two teams in one company, under the same policies, can differ sharply, so the unit that matters is the group rather than the person or the firm.
